name: Kingdom of England
summary: The kingdom united by Æthelstan in 927; conquered by the Normans in 1066, it developed Parliament and common law, broke with Rome (1534), ruled Wales and Ireland, and joined Scotland to form Great Britain in 1707.

location.value: England; Edward I effectively conquered Wales in 1282 and the Laws in Wales Acts of 1535–1542 fully united England and Wales; William II annexed Cumbria in 1092, Henry I ceded Lothian in 1124, and Calais was lost in 1558.

terrain.value: Mostly lowland plains and rolling hills, with moors in the north and south-west and long coasts.

climate.value: Mild and wet, shaped by the Atlantic, with no extreme heat or cold.

resources.value: Wool, tin from Cornwall, lead, coal and good farmland; later iron and coal helped industry.

disasters.value: The Great Fire of London (1666) destroyed much of the old city; the Black Death and harvest failures also caused great loss.

population.value: The page gives no population figures (the Domesday and 1700 figures are not stated there).

urbanisation.value: London grew to over 500,000 people by 1700; Norwich, Bristol and York were other major towns.

disease.value: The Black Death (1348–49) killed perhaps a third to a half of the people; plague returned many times, including London in 1665.

migration.value: Normans came after 1066, Flemish weavers in the Middle Ages, and Huguenot refugees from France in the 1600s.

economicBase.value: Not described on the page. It mentions only royal taxes (the geld) and sheriffs' payments, and says London became England's chief commercial centre after the Norman Conquest. Farming and the wool trade need another source.

tradeRoutes.value: Wool and cloth went to Flanders and the Low Countries; from the 1500s English ships traded across the Atlantic and to India.

wealth.value: Merchant wealth grew steadily from the wool trade, and later from overseas trade and colonies.

moneyAndTax.value: The silver penny and later the pound sterling; Parliament voted taxes, and kings struggled over how much to ask.

inequality.value: A society of great lords, gentry, townspeople and a large number of poor peasants and labourers.

governmentType.value: A monarchy with a Parliament; Magna Carta was sealed on 15 June 1215. The page does not mention the 1649–1660 republic.

keyRulers.value: Æthelstan conquered York, the last Viking kingdom, in 927; William I was crowned on 25 December 1066; Henry II reigned 1154–1189 and Elizabeth I 1558–1603.

succession.value: Hereditary; disputed in the Wars of the Roses.

institutions.value: Parliament; common law; Bill of Rights (1689).

eliteConflict.value: The crown clashed with barons (Magna Carta, 1215) and with Parliament, leading to the Civil War (1642–51).

armyAndTech.value: Longbowmen won battles such as Crécy (1346) and Agincourt (1415); from the 1500s a powerful navy defended the island.

majorWars.value: The Hundred Years’ War (1337–1453), the Wars of the Roses (1455–1487) and the English Civil War (1641–1645 on the page, ending in the king’s defeat).

alliancesRivals.value: France was the long-running rival; in the 1500s–1600s Spain and the Dutch Republic also challenged England.

openness.value: Open to trade and ideas from Europe, though hostile to Catholics after the Reformation.

communicationTransport.value: Roads, rivers and the sea carried goods and messages; canals and turnpike roads improved travel in the 1700s.

languageWriting.value: Old English, then Middle and modern English.

artsArchitecture.value: Gothic cathedrals such as Canterbury and Salisbury, Elizabethan theatre and Shakespeare, and Wren’s churches after the Great Fire.

socialStructure.value: Feudal at first, with lords, knights and serfs; later a gentry, merchants and yeomen, with a growing middle class.

sharedIdentity.value: An English identity tied to the crown, the common law, Parliament and, after 1534, Protestant faith.

dailyLife.value: Most people lived in farming villages, ate bread, pottage and ale, and followed the seasons and the church calendar.

neighbours.value: Scotland, Wales, Ireland and, across the Channel, France.

colonisation.value: Annexed Wales under the Laws in Wales Acts of 1535–1542, creating full union of England and Wales.

riseSignals.value: Unified when Æthelstan conquered York on 12 July 927.

peakPeriod.value: Elizabeth I reigned 1558–1603; the navy defeated the Spanish Armada in 1588 and her reign laid the foundations of the British Empire. The page dates the kingdom from 927 (Æthelstan) to 1 May 1707 (Acts of Union).

declineSignals.value: No decline as such: it united with Scotland to form the Kingdom of Great Britain in 1707.

outcome.value: The Norman Conquest (Battle of Hastings, 14 October 1066) moved the capital to Westminster. The kingdom ended on 1 May 1707 with the Acts of Union.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are well documented; population figures are estimates.
